extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in inter partes review (petitioners, patent owners), and administrative patent judges
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a petitioner has shown a reasonable likelihood of prevailing that claimed patent claims are unpatentable as obvious over asserted prior-art references, including claim-element mapping, motivation-to-combine, and construing spatial/structural claim limitations for institution decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution threshold — reasonable likelihood of prevailing
rubrics_metrics.description: For institution the petitioner must show a reasonable likelihood that it would prevail in demonstrating unpatentability (e.g., obviousness) of the challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates the record at the institution stage on whether Petitioner 'sufficiently shows for the purposes of institution' a reasonable likelihood of success. Language used: 'sufficiently shows for the purposes of institution' and 'there is a reasonable likelihood that Petitioner will prevail'. This is the standard applied to decide whether to institute review on asserted grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — teachings and motivation to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, Petitioner must demonstrate that the prior art references teach or suggest the claimed limitations and that a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would have had a motivation or reason to combine those references to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support can include expert testimony and specific citations to the references (paragraphs, figures). The asserted combination should yield predictable results. Courts/Board recognize that a course of action may have simultaneous advantages and disadvantages, and disadvantages do not necessarily obviate motivation to combine (Medichem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping prior-art structures to claimed elements (single-structure mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mapping structures in a prior-art reference to claimed elements, a petitioner must support the mapping; Patent Owner may argue that a single structure cannot satisfy two distinct claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becton, Dickinson established that separately recited claim elements ordinarily indicate separate components; but Google v. EcoFactor clarified that this is a rebuttable presumption — separately listed limitations may but do not always require separate physical structures. The intrinsic record (specification/claims) can rebut the presumption if it permits a single structure to satisfy multiple claim limitations. Provide intrinsic support or expert testimony if arguing a single prior-art structure meets multiple limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and reliance on the intrinsic record
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope and required structural features of claim limitations are determined by the intrinsic record (claim language, specification, figures) and may limit whether prior-art structures read on the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent's specification defines or narrows a term (e.g., 'first connector' requiring only 'an electrically conductive terminal'), the Board will interpret claims accordingly. Petitioners should show that the intrinsic record does not preclude their mapping; Patent Owners may rely on figures and specification language to require distinct structural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial/positional claim-limitation interpretation (e.g., 'on one side of the body')
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatial claim language (such as requiring a power socket and connector 'on one side of the body' and a second connector 'on another side') must be interpreted with reference to the patent's disclosure and figures; asserted prior art must be shown to teach the same spatial arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patent figures, specification text, and prior claim-construction positions (e.g., district court constructions) to determine whether a reference discloses the required spatial relationships. Disputes over whether a prior-art connector is on the 'same side' may hinge on how the term 'side' or orientation is used in the intrinsic record and cited prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and weight of evidence types at institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence to support obviousness grounds at institution typically includes annotated figures, expert declarations, cited paragraphs/figures from prior art, and translations where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions commonly rely on annotated drawings of prior-art references, expert testimony (e.g., Dr. Wolfe) explaining mappings and motivations, and citations to specific paragraphs/figures. The Board assesses whether this evidence collectively supports the asserted teaching/motivation for institution purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show that a combination cures deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining multiple references, the petitioner must show the combination supplies teachings missing from one reference such that the combination, as a whole, teaches the claim limitation(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how a second (or further) reference provides the particular structure or positioning lacking in the primary reference and why a PHOSITA would apply that teaching to the primary reference. Cite explicit structural teachings (figures, paragraphs) and expert rationale for the combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of relying on common design choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Board may accept as a basis for modifications claims that certain changes (e.g., splitting signals between connectors or moving connectors to different edges) are matters of simple design choice available to a PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support with expert testimony and citations to references showing the design choice is common or routine in the art. Show that such a modification would not materially affect operation and would yield predictable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior litigation claim-construction positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim-construction positions taken by parties in district court litigation (e.g., how 'on one side of the body' was defined) may be cited in IPR to support interpretations of claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may consider those positions but will ultimately construe claims based on the intrinsic record and applicable law. Parties should cite and explain how prior constructions align with or differ from the intrinsic disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board institution scope rule (SAS/37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board institutes review, it authorizes the review to proceed on all of the challenged claims and on all grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu and 37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a). If institution is granted on some claims/grounds, institution necessarily extends to all challenged claims and grounds in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble teaching and limiting effect (doctrine of claim preamble)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the petitioner demonstrates the prior art teaches the claim preamble, the Board need not resolve at institution whether the preamble is a limiting claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Nidec: when preamble is shown to be taught by the prior art, institution can proceed without determining if the preamble is limiting. If preamble is in dispute, show that the preamble is taught by the references or rely on intrinsic record for limitation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of figures/annotations — avoid impermissible cross-device mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated figures are useful to show correspondence between prior art and claimed structure, but care must be taken not to impermissibly attribute elements of one device/fan in a figure to different devices or to mis-map which element belongs to which claimed unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using annotated multi-unit drawings (e.g., chains of fans), explicitly explain the mapping and ensure the mapping aligns with the claim language (e.g., which connector belongs to which fan body). Patent Owner arguments often focus on alleged mis-mapping across adjacent devices; address such objections with clear annotation and explanation.
